newsitem.title: FRANCE: French left, right gird for immigration battle.
newsitem.headline: French left, right gird for immigration battle.

text.p: The French left and the ruling conservatives are preparing for a weekend battle in the streets over a bitterly disputed immigration bill, with the extreme-right National Front looming in the background.

Civil rights groups, film personalities, intellectuals, left-wing parties and trade unions plan a show of strength with a march in Paris on Saturday before the bill is given a second reading in the National Assembly next Tuesday.

The protesters, including Danielle Mitterrand, widow of the late Socialist president, accuse the government of pandering to the National Front, and to racism and xenophobia. They are demanding the withdrawal of the legislation.

The centre-right government insists there is no longer any reason to demonstrate since it has agreed to remove a disputed clause that would have obliged French hosts to notify the police when foreign guests from developing countries left their homes.

"The controversy is changing in nature. The problems which had upset some people, the risk of having to report (foreigners) to the police no longer exists with the amendment adopted by the parliamentary legislation committee," government spokesman Alain Lamassoure told reporters.
Some campaigners were now calling into question the very principle of fighting against illegal immigration, he said.
The parliamentary committee passed an amendment on Thursday that would make foreigners on short-term visas responsible for reporting their own departure to the authorities.

But the issue has turned into the kind of ideological battle which the French love to fight, with each side accusing the other of playing into the hands of anti-immigration crusader Jean-Marie Le Pen, leader of the National Front.

President Jacques Chirac's Gaullist RPR party said its members would distribute two million leaflets on Saturday defending the bill, which is intended to crack down on illegal immigration and close loopholes in past laws.

An opinion poll showed that 59 percent of voters supported the original bill proposed by Interior Minister Jean-Louis Debre, including the obligation on citizens to report the departure of foreigners to the police.

However Prime Minister Alain Juppe agreed to amend that article after more than 15,000 film makers, actors, academics, writers and professionals signed petitions denouncing it and calling for civil disobedience.

Film star Isabelle Adjani, daughter of an Algerian father, joined the ranks of protesters on Friday, telling the newspaper Le Monde: "We have to act together to kill this serpent in its egg. Yes, this bill really is a serpent's egg...Its authors are playing with fire."
Le Monde published a supplement honouring immigrants on Friday entitled, in a reference to the principles underpinning the French state, "Liberty, equality and fraternity for all".

A leader of the Jewish community, while voicing opposition to any measure that would involve denouncing people to the police, warned critics against comparing the Debre bill to the anti-Jewish laws of France's wartime collaborationist Vichy government.

Jean Kahn, president of the main Jewish religious body, the Consistoire Central Israelite de France, said there was no justification for comparing "the present day when democratic republican institutions are at work, and an era when the basic values of liberty, equality and fraternity were flouted".
Le Pen told a rally on Thursday night that the Debre bill was "a political manoeuvre aimed not at solving the problem of immigration but merely at fighting the National Front".

He renewed his call for radical measures to end immigrants' right of family reunification, abolish a law under which all children born on French soil are entitled to French citizenship and introduce a preference for French and European nationals in jobs, housing and family allowances.
